title: Adulting
meaning: Adulting means doing ordinary responsibilities associated with being an independent adult, especially when they feel annoyingly grown-up.
example: "I paid taxes and booked a dentist appointment. Serious adulting today."
context: The word is usually humorous and is popular among younger adults dealing with bills, cooking, admin and other everyday responsibilities.

title: AFK
meaning: AFK stands for “away from keyboard” and means someone is temporarily not active at their computer or game.
example: "AFK for five minutes - food's here."
context: The term came from online chat and gaming but is still widely used even when nobody is literally using a keyboard.

title: Afterparty
meaning: An afterparty is a party or gathering that continues after the main event has ended.
example: "The club closed, so everyone went to an afterparty."
context: Afterparties are usually smaller and later than the main event and can happen at a house, hotel, bar or another venue.

title: Algorithm
meaning: An algorithm is the system a platform uses to decide what content to recommend, rank or show to each user.
example: "I watched one running clip and the algorithm gave me fifty more."
context: On social media, people often say “the algorithm” as shorthand for the recommendation systems behind feeds such as TikTok’s For You Page or Instagram Reels.

title: All-nighter
meaning: An all-nighter is a night spent staying awake instead of sleeping, usually to study, work or finish something urgent.
example: "We pulled an all-nighter to finish the project."
context: All-nighters are a classic student cliché, but lack of sleep usually makes concentration and performance worse the next day.

title: Alt account
meaning: An alt account is an alternative social-media account separate from someone’s main profile.
example: "I only post random stuff on my alt."
context: An alt may be more private, more niche or used for a different audience. Unlike a burner, it does not have to be anonymous or temporary.

title: ASAP
meaning: ASAP stands for “as soon as possible.”
example: "Can you send the file ASAP?"
context: The abbreviation is common in work, school and everyday messages. It signals urgency, although the actual deadline may still need clarification.

title: Assignment
meaning: An assignment is a piece of work a student is required to complete for a course.
example: "The assignment is due Friday at five."
context: Assignments can include essays, reports, presentations, coding tasks, problem sets and many other forms of assessed or practice work.

title: Ate
meaning: Ate means someone performed extremely well, looked amazing or completely nailed something.
example: "She ate that presentation."
context: The expression comes from the idea that someone “devoured” a performance or look. It is common in fashion, music, dance and social media.

title: Ate and left no crumbs
meaning: Ate and left no crumbs is exaggerated praise meaning someone did something so well there was nothing left to improve.
example: "That final dance routine? She ate and left no crumbs."
context: It is a stronger, more playful version of saying someone ate.

title: Aura
meaning: Aura is slang for the cool, confident or impressive energy someone gives off.
example: "Walking into the party in sunglasses at midnight gave him ridiculous aura."
context: Online, aura is treated almost like an invisible social score. Doing something effortlessly cool can give you aura, while an awkward moment can make you “lose aura.”

title: Aura points
meaning: Aura points are imaginary points people gain or lose based on how cool, confident or embarrassing their actions seem.
example: "Catching the bottle without looking? Plus 1,000 aura points."
context: The phrase is usually used jokingly on TikTok and in memes. There is no real score: people simply award or subtract points to rate someone’s vibe or social performance.

title: Bar crawl
meaning: A bar crawl is an outing where a group visits several bars in one evening, usually having a drink at each stop.
example: "We planned a bar crawl through the city centre."
context: The route may be organised in advance or improvised. Large organised crawls sometimes use themes, tickets or matching shirts.

title: Based
meaning: Based describes an opinion or person seen as confidently authentic, especially when they do not care whether others agree.
example: "He said exactly what everyone was thinking. Based."
context: Online, the word is often used as a one-word sign of approval. Because it appears in many internet communities, the tone can range from sincere to ironic.

title: Beer pong
meaning: Beer pong is a party game where players throw ping-pong balls toward cups arranged on a table.
example: "We somehow won three beer pong games in a row."
context: House rules vary a lot. Traditionally, landing a ball in a cup means the other team drinks, although people also play with water in the cups and separate drinks.

title: Before and after
meaning: Before and after content shows how something or someone looked before a change and how it looks afterward.
example: "The room makeover before and after is insane."
context: The format is common for fitness, fashion, cleaning, renovations, haircuts and glow-ups because it makes the transformation easy to compare.

title: Beige flag
meaning: A beige flag is a harmless but slightly odd or boring trait that is neither a serious positive nor a serious warning sign.
example: "His beige flag is that he rates every supermarket he visits."
context: The term became popular as a humorous middle ground between red and green flags, especially in relationship content.

title: Benching
meaning: Benching means keeping someone as a backup dating option while giving them just enough attention to stay interested.
example: "He only texts when his other plans fall through. I'm being benched."
context: Like a substitute player waiting on the bench, the person is kept available without being made a real priority.

title: Bet
meaning: Bet is an informal way to say “okay,” “deal” or “sounds good.”
example: "Meet at nine? Bet."
context: It can also be used as a challenge, similar to saying “watch me” or “you'll see.” The intended meaning is normally obvious from the conversation.

title: Big mood
meaning: Big mood is a stronger version of mood, used when something feels extremely relatable.
example: "Ordering dessert before dinner? Big mood."
context: It is intentionally exaggerated and is most often used humorously in comments and messages.

title: Blacked out
meaning: Blacked out means experiencing an alcohol-related memory blackout.
example: "She was still talking and walking, but later realised she'd blacked out."
context: Because someone can appear conscious during a blackout, friends may not immediately notice it. Repeated blackouts are a strong warning sign around alcohol use.

title: Blackout
meaning: A blackout is a period of memory loss caused by heavy alcohol consumption, even though the person may have remained awake.
example: "He remembers arriving at the club, but everything after that is a blackout."
context: A blackout is not the same as passing out. It is a serious sign of very high intoxication and can come with significant safety risks.

title: Body count
meaning: Body count is slang for the number of people someone has had sex with.
example: "They spent the whole podcast arguing about body count."
context: The term can feel judgmental or objectifying, and people differ widely on whether they consider the number relevant. It originally had unrelated meanings, including a count of deaths.

title: Bottoms up
meaning: Bottoms up is a toast said just before people drink, often encouraging everyone to finish or take a good sip.
example: "Glasses up - bottoms up!"
context: The phrase is informal and festive and is commonly heard during toasts, shots and party games.

title: Bouncer
meaning: A bouncer is a security worker at a bar, club or event who controls entry and deals with safety problems.
example: "The bouncer checked everyone's ID at the door."
context: Bouncers may refuse entry, remove disruptive guests and help enforce venue rules.

title: Brainrot
meaning: Brainrot describes being mentally consumed by low-quality, repetitive or extremely online content.
example: "I've watched so many edits that I officially have brainrot."
context: It can refer to the content itself or the feeling that you have spent far too much time thinking about a meme, fandom or internet trend.

title: Breadcrumbing
meaning: Breadcrumbing means giving someone small amounts of attention to keep them interested without genuinely committing or moving the relationship forward.
example: "She sends a flirty message every two weeks but never wants to meet. That's breadcrumbing."
context: The “breadcrumbs” are enough to maintain hope, such as occasional likes, replies or vague plans, but not enough to build a real relationship.

title: Broke
meaning: Broke means having little or no money available.
example: "I can't do another expensive dinner this week; I'm broke."
context: It is informal and often temporary, especially in student slang. Someone can say they are broke even if they are not literally without any money.

title: Broke student
meaning: A broke student is the stereotype of a student with very little disposable money after paying for rent, tuition and everyday expenses.
example: "Instant noodles again - broke student life."
context: The phrase is used humorously around cheap meals, discounts, second-hand furniture and creative ways to stretch a student budget.

title: BTW
meaning: BTW stands for “by the way.”
example: "BTW, your charger is still at my place."
context: It introduces an extra thought or topic that is not directly connected to the previous sentence.

title: Bucket list
meaning: A bucket list is a list of experiences or goals someone hopes to complete during their lifetime.
example: "Seeing the Northern Lights is high on my bucket list."
context: The phrase comes from “kick the bucket,” an informal expression for dying, but modern bucket lists are usually upbeat collections of travel and life goals.

title: Burner account
meaning: A burner account is a temporary or secondary account used without clearly linking it to your main identity.
example: "He posted the opinion from a burner account."
context: Burners are often used for privacy, anonymous discussion or viewing content without using a main account. They can also be misused for harassment or deception.

title: Burnout
meaning: Burnout is a state of deep physical and emotional exhaustion caused by prolonged stress or overwork.
example: "By the end of the semester, I was completely burned out."
context: People often use the term for work or study stress. Real burnout can affect motivation, concentration and wellbeing and is more than simply feeling tired after a busy day.

title: Bussin
meaning: Bussin means extremely good, especially when talking about food.
example: "These fries are bussin."
context: The term comes from African American English and spread widely through memes and TikTok. It is most natural as enthusiastic praise rather than a neutral description.

title: Buying a round
meaning: Buying a round means paying for a drink for each person in your group.
example: "There are eight of us, so buying a round suddenly got expensive."
context: The custom works best when groups are small and people are drinking at a similar pace; nobody is required to join in.

title: BYOB
meaning: BYOB stands for “bring your own bottle” or “bring your own booze,” meaning guests should bring their own drinks.
example: "The house party is BYOB, so grab something on the way."
context: The abbreviation is common on invitations and event messages. In some restaurant contexts it can mean customers may bring their own alcohol, subject to local rules.

title: Campus
meaning: A campus is the area containing the buildings and grounds of a university or college.
example: "The library is on the other side of campus."
context: A campus may include classrooms, housing, sports facilities, cafés and social spaces, depending on the institution.

title: Cancel culture
meaning: Cancel culture refers to the practice of publicly withdrawing support from someone after controversial or harmful behavior.
example: "The debate quickly turned into an argument about cancel culture."
context: The phrase is politically and culturally contested. Supporters may view it as accountability, while critics may see it as disproportionate punishment or online mob behavior.

title: Cancelled
meaning: Cancelled describes a public figure or person facing widespread rejection after behavior people consider offensive or unacceptable.
example: "After those old messages resurfaced, everyone said he was cancelled."
context: Online cancellation can range from temporary criticism to real consequences such as losing work or followers. The term is often used loosely and sometimes ironically.

title: Canon event
meaning: A canon event is an experience that feels inevitable and important to someone’s personal story, even if it is embarrassing or painful.
example: "Let him date the terrible ex. It's a canon event."
context: The meme became popular after Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. Online it is often used jokingly for mistakes people supposedly need to experience themselves.

title: Cap
meaning: Cap means a lie, exaggeration or something that is not true.
example: "You ran a 5K in twelve minutes? That's cap."
context: Calling “cap” is a way of saying you do not believe someone. The opposite is no cap, which is used to stress that something is true.

title: Catfish
meaning: A catfish is someone who uses a fake or misleading online identity, especially to deceive people in dating or relationships.
example: "The photos weren't even his. He was a catfish."
context: Catfishing can involve fake names, stolen photos or major lies about identity. The term became widely known through online-dating stories and the TV show Catfish.

title: Catfishing
meaning: Catfishing is pretending to be someone else online, especially by using fake or misleading identity information to form a relationship.
example: "The profile used stolen photos, so the whole relationship was catfishing."
context: It can involve romance, money scams or attention seeking. The person doing it is often called a catfish.

title: Chaotic
meaning: Chaotic describes something messy, unpredictable or full of uncontrolled energy.
example: "Three missed trains and a spontaneous tattoo - chaotic day."
context: The term is often positive or affectionate online, especially when the disorder makes a story funnier or more memorable.

title: Cheers
meaning: Cheers is a common toast said before drinking and can also mean “thanks” in British English.
example: "Cheers to finishing exams!"
context: When used as a toast, people often raise or lightly clink their glasses before taking a sip.

title: Chronically online
meaning: Chronically online describes someone whose opinions, habits or language seem heavily shaped by spending too much time on the internet.
example: "Only someone chronically online would understand that argument."
context: The phrase is often used when online discussions feel disconnected from everyday life or when a person knows an unusually large amount of internet drama.

title: Chug
meaning: To chug means to drink something very quickly in large gulps.
example: "He tried to chug the whole bottle of water after the run."
context: The word can be used for any drink, although in party contexts it often refers to alcohol.

title: Clickbait
meaning: Clickbait is a headline, thumbnail or post designed mainly to make people click, often by exaggerating what the content contains.
example: "The title said 'You won't believe what happened,' but nothing happened. Pure clickbait."
context: Clickbait works by creating curiosity. It becomes misleading when the content does not deliver what the headline promises.

title: Clout
meaning: Clout means social influence, attention or status, especially online.
example: "He only posted it for clout."
context: Someone with clout has reach or influence. The word is often used critically when people appear to chase attention rather than act genuinely.

title: Clout chasing
meaning: Clout chasing means deliberately doing things mainly to gain attention, followers or social status.
example: "Starting fake drama for views is pure clout chasing."
context: It commonly refers to provocative posts, public feuds or associating with famous people just to increase visibility.

title: Clubbing
meaning: Clubbing means going to nightclubs to dance, drink and socialise.
example: "We haven't been clubbing in months."
context: The word refers to the activity rather than one specific venue and is especially common in British English.

title: Comfort food
meaning: Comfort food is food associated with warmth, familiarity or emotional reassurance rather than just nutrition.
example: "Mac and cheese is my ultimate comfort food."
context: What counts as comfort food is personal and often connected to childhood, family traditions or foods eaten when someone wants to feel better.

title: Comfort show
meaning: A comfort show is a TV series you rewatch because it feels familiar, relaxing or emotionally safe.
example: "I've seen it five times, but it's still my comfort show."
context: People often return to comfort shows when stressed because they already know the characters and what will happen.

title: Content creator
meaning: A content creator is someone who regularly makes digital content such as videos, photos, podcasts, articles or livestreams.
example: "She works full-time as a content creator."
context: Not every creator is an influencer. “Creator” focuses on making content, while “influencer” emphasizes the effect someone has on an audience.

title: Cooked
meaning: Cooked means that someone is in trouble, exhausted, finished or unlikely to recover from a situation.
example: "I have an exam at eight and haven't opened the book. I'm cooked."
context: The exact meaning depends on context. You can be cooked after a hard workout, cooked because you made a terrible decision, or say a team is cooked when it has almost no chance left.

title: Core memory
meaning: A core memory is an experience that feels deeply memorable and emotionally important.
example: "Watching the sunrise with everyone after graduation became a core memory."
context: The phrase was popularised by Inside Out. Online, it is often used for moments people believe they will remember for years.

title: Couple goals
meaning: Couple goals means a couple appears especially cute, supportive or aspirational.
example: "Matching Halloween costumes without being annoying? Couple goals."
context: It is very similar to relationship goals, but focuses more directly on the pair and how they behave together.

title: Cover charge
meaning: A cover charge is a fee paid to enter a bar, club, party or entertainment venue.
example: "The club has a ten-dollar cover charge after eleven."
context: The fee usually pays for access rather than drinks, though some events include a drink token or other benefit.

title: Cramming
meaning: Cramming means trying to learn a large amount of material in a very short time, usually just before an exam.
example: "I ignored the notes for six weeks and spent Sunday cramming."
context: It can help with short-term recall, but spaced study over time is generally better for actually retaining information.

title: Crash out
meaning: To crash out means to lose emotional control and react recklessly, angrily or dramatically.
example: "If this group project gets changed again, I'm going to crash out."
context: The phrase is often exaggerated for humor, but it can also describe genuinely impulsive behavior. Context matters because the seriousness can vary a lot.

title: Creator economy
meaning: The creator economy is the ecosystem in which individuals earn money from audiences through content, sponsorships, subscriptions, products and platforms.
example: "More students are trying to build a side income in the creator economy."
context: It includes influencers, streamers, newsletter writers, podcasters and many other people who build businesses around their own audience.

title: Cringe
meaning: Cringe describes something so awkward, embarrassing or forced that it makes you uncomfortable to watch.
example: "That fake motivational speech was painfully cringe."
context: The word can describe content, behavior or even your own past actions. Online, calling something cringe is a quick way of saying it feels socially embarrassing.

title: Cuffing season
meaning: Cuffing season is the period, usually during colder months, when people are said to become more interested in finding a relationship or regular partner.
example: "Summer was chaos, but now cuffing season has started."
context: The idea is partly a meme and partly a dating pattern: colder weather, holidays and more time indoors can make having a partner seem especially appealing.

title: DD
meaning: DD commonly stands for “designated driver” in nightlife and party contexts.
example: "Who's DD tonight?"
context: Because DD has other meanings in different contexts, the surrounding conversation normally makes it clear that it refers to the sober driver.

title: Dead
meaning: Dead means something is so funny, shocking or absurd that you are figuratively “dead.”
example: "That voice note has me dead."
context: It is usually not literal at all. Online, “I'm dead” often means “I cannot stop laughing.”

title: Deadline
meaning: A deadline is the latest time or date by which something must be submitted or completed.
example: "I thought the deadline was midnight, but it was five o'clock."
context: Student life revolves around deadlines for assignments, applications and projects, which is why calendars suddenly become very important.

title: Dealbreaker
meaning: A dealbreaker is a behavior, value or condition that makes you unwilling to continue a relationship or agreement.
example: "Smoking is a dealbreaker for me."
context: Unlike an ick, a dealbreaker is usually a clear boundary or incompatibility that genuinely matters to someone.

title: Deepfake
meaning: A deepfake is AI-generated or digitally manipulated media that makes a person appear to say or do something they did not actually say or do.
example: "The clip looked real, but it turned out to be a deepfake."
context: Deepfakes can be used for entertainment, but also for scams, misinformation and non-consensual content, so checking the source matters.

title: Define the relationship
meaning: To define the relationship means to talk openly about the status, expectations and future of a romantic connection.
example: "Before deleting the apps, they decided to define the relationship."
context: The conversation may cover labels, exclusivity, commitment and whether both people want the same thing.

title: Delulu
meaning: Delulu is a playful shortening of “delusional,” used for someone who believes something unrealistic because they really want it to be true.
example: "She liked my story twice, so obviously we're getting married. I'm staying delulu."
context: The term first became popular in online fandoms and later spread to dating, career and lifestyle jokes. It is often self-deprecating rather than a serious accusation.

title: Designated driver
meaning: A designated driver is the person in a group who agrees not to drink alcohol so they can drive others home safely.
example: "Sam is the designated driver tonight."
context: Groups usually choose the driver before going out so there is a clear plan for getting home without impaired driving.

title: Digital footprint
meaning: A digital footprint is the trail of information and activity you leave behind online.
example: "That old tweet is still part of your digital footprint."
context: Posts, comments, accounts, searches and public records can all contribute to it. Some parts disappear quickly, while others may remain searchable for years.

title: Dissertation
meaning: A dissertation is a long academic research project written as part of a university degree.
example: "I spent most of spring in the library finishing my dissertation."
context: In some education systems a dissertation is associated with undergraduate or master’s study, while in others the terminology differs from thesis.

title: Dive bar
meaning: A dive bar is a casual, usually inexpensive bar with a simple, unpolished atmosphere.
example: "The fancy cocktail place was full, so we ended up in a great dive bar."
context: The term can sound negative, but many people use it affectionately for bars that feel authentic, relaxed and free of pretension.

title: DM
meaning: DM stands for “direct message,” a private message sent to another user on a social platform.
example: "Send me the address in a DM."
context: The term is used across Instagram, X, TikTok and other platforms. It can refer to the message itself or the act of messaging privately.

title: Doomscrolling
meaning: Doomscrolling is continuously scrolling through negative news or upsetting content even though it makes you feel worse.
example: "I opened my phone for one update and ended up doomscrolling for an hour."
context: The term became especially common during periods of major news and crisis. It describes the hard-to-stop loop of consuming bad news online.

title: Dorm
meaning: A dorm is a building or room where students live, especially at an American college or university.
example: "My dorm is tiny, but at least it's close to class."
context: Dorm is short for dormitory. In British English, terms such as halls or student accommodation are more common.

title: Dorm room
meaning: A dorm room is a student bedroom inside a dormitory or residence hall.
example: "We somehow fit two beds, two desks and a fridge into one dorm room."
context: Dorm rooms are often shared and are usually part of larger student housing with communal spaces or facilities.

title: Double texting
meaning: Double texting means sending another message before the other person has replied to your previous one.
example: "I forgot to send the address, so I had to double text."
context: It is completely normal in many conversations, although dating culture sometimes treats it as a sign that someone is overly eager.

title: Down bad
meaning: Down bad means being desperately attracted to someone or being in a particularly rough situation.
example: "He's liked every photo she posted since 2018. He's down bad."
context: Online, the phrase is especially common for embarrassing levels of romantic or sexual interest, but it can also mean generally struggling.

title: Dragged
meaning: Being dragged means being heavily criticized or mocked, especially by many people online.
example: "He posted the bad take and got dragged in the comments."
context: The word suggests the criticism is intense and public, often after a controversial post or obvious mistake.

title: Drinking game
meaning: A drinking game is a game in which players drink according to rules, results or mistakes.
example: "They turned the movie into a drinking game."
context: Examples include beer pong, Kings Cup and Flip Cup. Because drinking games can encourage fast consumption, people should keep track of how much they actually drink.

title: Drip
meaning: Drip means stylish clothes, accessories or an overall fashionable look.
example: "New jacket, new shoes - the drip is serious today."
context: Someone with drip has a strong sense of style. The word is especially associated with streetwear, hip-hop and internet culture.

title: Dropout
meaning: A dropout is someone who leaves a school, university or course before completing it.
example: "He became a college dropout after leaving to start a company."
context: The word can be neutral in some contexts but may sound judgmental in others. People leave education for many different personal, financial or career reasons.

title: Dry texting
meaning: Dry texting is replying with very short, low-effort messages that make a conversation difficult to continue.
example: "I ask full questions and all I get back is 'yeah' or 'lol.' The dry texting is painful."
context: One-word answers, no follow-up questions and little emotion can make someone seem uninterested, although some people simply have a brief texting style.

title: DTR
meaning: DTR stands for “define the relationship.”
example: "We've been dating for two months. I think it's time for a DTR."
context: A DTR conversation is when people discuss what their connection actually is, whether they are exclusive and what they expect from each other.

title: Duet
meaning: A Duet is a TikTok feature that lets you post your video next to another user’s video in a split-screen format.
example: "I dueted the original clip with my reaction."
context: Duets are commonly used for reactions, challenges, singing, commentary and jokes. The original video stays visible alongside the new one.

title: Elective
meaning: An elective is a course a student can choose rather than one that is strictly required by their programme.
example: "I took photography as an elective."
context: Electives give students room to explore another interest, specialise within a degree or earn required credits more flexibly.

title: Engagement bait
meaning: Engagement bait is content designed mainly to make people like, comment, share or react so that the platform shows it to more users.
example: "Comment your birth month below" is classic engagement bait."
context: Questions, controversial opinions and “tag a friend” prompts can all be engagement bait. It becomes annoying when interaction matters more than the content itself.

title: Era
meaning: An era is a distinct phase or period in someone’s life, style or interests.
example: "I'm officially in my early-morning gym era."
context: Social media uses the word playfully to turn even short phases into dramatic chapters of personal identity.

title: Exchange student
meaning: An exchange student studies temporarily at an institution in another country as part of an exchange programme.
example: "Our new exchange student is here from Denmark for one semester."
context: Exchange students usually remain connected to their home university while taking courses and experiencing student life abroad.

title: Exclusive
meaning: Exclusive means two people have agreed not to date or pursue other people romantically or sexually.
example: "We're not officially calling each other boyfriend and girlfriend yet, but we are exclusive."
context: Exclusivity can be part of a committed relationship, but some couples agree to it before choosing a formal label.

title: FaceTune
meaning: FaceTune is a photo-editing app whose name is often used more generally for heavily retouching selfies or portraits.
example: "That photo looks so FaceTuned I barely recognize him."
context: People associate the app with smoothing skin, reshaping features and changing proportions. Using “FaceTuned” as slang usually implies that an image has been edited a lot.

title: Facts
meaning: Facts is an emphatic way to say that a statement is true or that you completely agree.
example: "Group projects are always more work than expected." - "Facts."
context: It is often used as a one-word reaction, similar to “exactly” or “so true.”

title: Filter
meaning: A filter is a digital effect that changes the appearance of a photo or video.
example: "Which filter did you use on that story?"
context: Filters can adjust color and lighting or add face effects, backgrounds and augmented-reality elements. On social platforms they can range from subtle edits to complete transformations.

title: FinSta
meaning: FinSta means “fake Instagram,” usually a private secondary Instagram account shared with a smaller, trusted group.
example: "The polished photos go on main; the chaos goes on the FinSta."
context: Despite the word “fake,” a FinSta is often where people post more candid or personal content than on their public account.

title: Fire
meaning: Fire means excellent, exciting or very good.
example: "That new track is fire."
context: It is a broad compliment used for music, food, outfits, parties and almost anything else people think is impressive.

title: Fit check
meaning: A fit check is a quick look at or review of someone’s outfit.
example: "Before we go in: fit check."
context: “Fit” is short for outfit. Fit checks often appear as mirror videos, group clips or quick shots showing clothes, shoes and accessories.

title: Flatmate
meaning: A flatmate is someone who lives in the same flat or apartment as you.
example: "My flatmate is cooking tonight, so I'm doing the dishes."
context: The term is especially common in British English. It is similar to roommate, but does not imply sharing the same bedroom.

title: Flex
meaning: A flex is something you show off because you are proud of it or want other people to notice.
example: "Casually mentioning your first-class upgrade is such a flex."
context: To flex can mean showing off money, skills, achievements, connections or anything else that signals status.

title: Flip cup
meaning: Flip cup is a team drinking game where players drink from a cup and then try to flip it upside down by flicking its edge.
example: "Our side lost the flip cup final in about thirty seconds."
context: Each player normally has to finish their turn before the next teammate starts, making it a fast relay-style party game.

title: FML
meaning: FML stands for “fuck my life” and expresses frustration, embarrassment or bad luck.
example: "I left my keys inside and the door locked behind me. FML."
context: It is informal and vulgar, usually used dramatically rather than literally when something annoying goes wrong.

title: FOMO
meaning: FOMO stands for “fear of missing out,” the anxious feeling that other people are having rewarding experiences without you.
example: "I was exhausted, but FOMO convinced me to go to the party."
context: Social media can intensify FOMO because you constantly see highlights from other people’s lives and events.

title: For You Page
meaning: The For You Page is TikTok’s personalized feed where the platform recommends videos based on what it thinks you will enjoy.
example: "My For You Page is suddenly nothing but running videos."
context: It is the main discovery feed on TikTok and is shaped by signals such as watch time, likes, shares and other interactions.

title: Frat
meaning: Frat is an informal shortening of fraternity.
example: "The frat is hosting a charity event this weekend."
context: It is also used in phrases such as frat party and “frat house.” Some fraternity members prefer the full word.

title: Frat party
meaning: A frat party is a party organised by or held at a college fraternity, particularly in the United States.
example: "Half the campus seemed to be at the frat party."
context: The term is strongly associated with American college culture and may involve fraternity houses, large crowds and student nightlife.

title: Fraternity
meaning: A fraternity is a membership-based student organisation, especially at US colleges, traditionally associated with male members.
example: "He joined a fraternity in his first semester."
context: Fraternities can focus on social life, networking, service or professional interests. Social fraternities are part of what is often called Greek life.

title: Fresher
meaning: A fresher is a first-year university student, especially in British English.
example: "Every fresher eventually learns which campus café is cheapest."
context: It is roughly comparable to the American freshman, although the education systems and usage are different.

title: Freshers
meaning: Freshers are students who have just started university, especially in the United Kingdom.
example: "The society is organising a welcome event for freshers."
context: The term is the plural of fresher and is strongly associated with the first weeks of university life in the UK.

title: Freshers' Week
meaning: Freshers’ Week is the welcome period for new university students before or around the start of classes, especially in the UK.
example: "I joined three societies during Freshers' Week and quit two by October."
context: Universities and student unions use the week for introductions, parties, club fairs and practical information about campus life.

title: Freshman
meaning: A freshman is a student in the first year of high school or college in the United States.
example: "As a freshman, I got lost on campus every day for the first week."
context: The word is especially American. Some institutions prefer gender-neutral alternatives such as “first-year student.”

title: Friends with benefits
meaning: Friends with benefits are friends who also have a sexual relationship without being a committed romantic couple.
example: "We get along well, but it's just friends with benefits."
context: The arrangement depends on clear expectations because friendship, sex and romantic feelings can become mixed if both people want different things.

title: Friendzone
meaning: The friendzone describes a situation where one person wants a romantic relationship but the other person only sees them as a friend.
example: "I finally asked her out, but she said she only sees me as a friend."
context: The word is usually used informally. Friendship is not a punishment or something someone owes their way out of, so the term is best understood as describing mismatched romantic interest.

title: FYI
meaning: FYI stands for “for your information.”
example: "FYI, the meeting moved to three."
context: It is used to share information someone may need to know. Depending on tone, it can sound helpful, neutral or slightly sharp.

title: FYP
meaning: FYP stands for “For You Page,” TikTok’s personalized feed of recommended videos.
example: "This video somehow ended up all over my FYP."
context: People also use #fyp in captions hoping their content will be recommended more widely, although the hashtag itself does not guarantee reach.

title: Gap year
meaning: A gap year is a period, often around a year, taken between stages of education or before starting work.
example: "She took a gap year to travel and work in Australia."
context: People use gap years for travel, volunteering, work or personal projects before continuing university or a career path.

title: Gaslighting
meaning: Gaslighting means manipulating someone into doubting their own memory, perception or judgment.
example: "He denied saying it even though the message was right there, then told her she was imagining things."
context: The term comes from the story Gas Light. Online it is sometimes overused for ordinary disagreement, but true gaslighting involves a pattern of psychological manipulation.

title: Ghost account
meaning: A ghost account is an account that exists but has little visible activity, personal information or original content.
example: "That profile has no posts and follows 900 people - total ghost account."
context: People use ghost accounts to browse quietly, protect privacy or separate their viewing habits from their main profile.

title: Ghosting
meaning: Ghosting means suddenly stopping all communication with someone without giving an explanation.
example: "We were texting every day and then he just ghosted me."
context: It is especially common as a dating term, but people can also ghost friends, recruiters or work contacts. The key feature is disappearing rather than clearly ending the interaction.

title: Giving
meaning: Giving means suggesting, resembling or creating a particular vibe.
example: "The tiny sunglasses are giving 2000s pop star."
context: It is often used before a comparison and works similarly to “this reminds me of...” in a more playful way.

title: Glazing
meaning: Glazing means praising someone so excessively that it starts to look embarrassing or dishonest.
example: "You called him a genius five times in one minute. Stop glazing."
context: It is mainly used online when someone appears to admire a celebrity, athlete or creator far more than necessary.

title: Glow-up
meaning: A glow-up is a noticeable positive transformation in someone’s appearance, confidence, lifestyle or overall vibe.
example: "His first-year-to-graduation glow-up is unreal."
context: The term is often used for before-and-after comparisons. A glow-up can be physical, but it can also refer to becoming happier, healthier or more confident.

title: GOAT
meaning: GOAT stands for “Greatest Of All Time” and is used for someone considered the best in their field.
example: "Messi is the GOAT, don't argue with me."
context: It started as a sports-heavy acronym but is now used for musicians, creators, friends, food and almost anything people want to praise at the highest level.

title: Going viral
meaning: Going viral means a post, video or idea suddenly spreading to a very large audience online.
example: "He uploaded the clip before bed and woke up to find it going viral."
context: Virality usually involves unusually fast growth in views, shares or mentions compared with a creator’s normal reach.

title: GPA
meaning: GPA stands for “Grade Point Average,” a numerical summary of academic performance used especially in the United States.
example: "The scholarship requires a minimum GPA."
context: Schools calculate GPA using grades converted into points. The exact scale and weighting system can differ between institutions.

title: Green flag
meaning: A green flag is a positive sign that someone may be trustworthy, compatible or emotionally healthy.
example: "He remembered the little things I told him. Green flag."
context: The phrase is the positive counterpart to red flag and is often used for respectful communication, reliability and thoughtful behavior.

title: Group project
meaning: A group project is an assignment completed by several students working together.
example: "The group project somehow became one person doing the slides at midnight."
context: Group projects are meant to build collaboration, but they are also famous for uneven workloads, scheduling problems and chaotic group chats.

title: GRWM
meaning: GRWM stands for “Get Ready With Me,” a video format where someone films themselves getting dressed, doing makeup or preparing for an event.
example: "GRWM for my first date in six months."
context: Creators often talk to the camera while getting ready, turning the format into a mix of fashion, beauty, storytelling and casual conversation.

title: Guest list
meaning: A guest list is a list of people approved or invited to enter an event or venue.
example: "We're on the guest list, so don't lose the confirmation."
context: Being on a guest list can mean guaranteed entry, a shorter queue, discounted admission or free access, depending on the venue.

title: Guilty pleasure
meaning: A guilty pleasure is something you enjoy even though you feel it is embarrassing, uncool or not especially high quality.
example: "Terrible reality TV is my guilty pleasure."
context: The “guilt” is usually playful. It can refer to food, music, films, shows or any interest someone enjoys despite judging it a little.

title: Hair of the dog
meaning: Hair of the dog is the idea of drinking more alcohol to reduce hangover symptoms.
example: "Someone suggested a beer as hair of the dog, but I chose coffee instead."
context: The expression is old, but drinking more only delays recovery and can add more alcohol to your system rather than actually fixing the hangover.

title: Hangover
meaning: A hangover is the unpleasant physical and mental feeling that can follow drinking too much alcohol.
example: "I woke up with a brutal hangover after the party."
context: Common symptoms include headache, thirst, nausea, tiredness and poor concentration. Time, hydration and rest help more reliably than supposed miracle cures.

title: Happy hour
meaning: Happy hour is a period when a bar or restaurant offers discounted drinks or other specials.
example: "We got there just before happy hour ended."
context: Despite the name, it can last longer than one hour. Rules around alcohol promotions differ between places and countries.

title: Hard launch
meaning: A hard launch is a clear, public announcement that removes any mystery about something new.
example: "After months of hints, they finally hard launched the relationship with a couple photo."
context: It is the opposite of a soft launch. In dating, the partner is openly shown or named; in business, the release is fully promoted.

title: Hater
meaning: A hater is someone who regularly criticizes, dislikes or tries to bring down another person.
example: "Ignore the comments. Every creator gets haters."
context: The term is often used casually and can sometimes be a way of dismissing criticism rather than engaging with it.

title: Heavyweight
meaning: A heavyweight, in drinking slang, is someone believed to tolerate a larger amount of alcohol before appearing drunk.
example: "Everyone calls him a heavyweight, but he still needs to know his limits."
context: Alcohol tolerance does not make heavy drinking safe. Someone can look less affected while still having a high blood alcohol level.

title: Highkey
meaning: Highkey means openly, strongly or very obviously.
example: "I highkey need a holiday after this week."
context: It is basically the louder opposite of lowkey. People use it when they are not trying to hide how strongly they feel about something.

title: Hookup
meaning: A hookup is a casual romantic or sexual encounter without necessarily implying a committed relationship.
example: "They met at the party and hooked up later."
context: The exact meaning can vary from kissing to sex, so people often rely on context rather than assuming one specific activity.

title: Hot take
meaning: A hot take is a strong or controversial opinion, often stated to provoke discussion.
example: "Hot take: brunch is just overpriced breakfast."
context: Online, people use the phrase before opinions they expect others to disagree with. Sometimes the “hot take” is deliberately exaggerated for engagement.

title: House party
meaning: A house party is a social gathering held in someone’s home rather than at a bar, club or formal venue.
example: "We skipped the club and ended up at a house party instead."
context: House parties can range from a few friends in a living room to crowded student events. They are a staple of student and youth nightlife.

title: Hungover
meaning: Hungover means suffering from a hangover after drinking alcohol.
example: "I'm too hungover to look at a screen right now."
context: It is the adjective form of hangover and is often used the morning after a party or night out.

title: Hustle culture
meaning: Hustle culture is the idea that people should constantly work, optimise and chase success, often at the expense of rest.
example: "Turning every hobby into a side hustle is peak hustle culture."
context: The phrase is often critical of social-media messages that glorify long hours, nonstop productivity and tying personal worth to achievement.

title: I'm weak
meaning: I'm weak means something is extremely funny or has made you lose composure from laughing.
example: "He tried to dance and immediately fell over. I'm weak."
context: It is similar to I'm dead and is commonly used in messages, comments and reaction posts.

title: Ick
meaning: An ick is a small behavior or trait that suddenly makes someone less attractive to you.
example: "He clapped when the plane landed and I got the ick."
context: Icks are often irrational and highly personal. They usually describe a sudden turn-off rather than a genuinely serious problem.

title: IDC
meaning: IDC stands for “I don't care.”
example: "Pick whichever restaurant you want, IDC."
context: Because the phrase can sound blunt, context matters. Among friends it may simply mean someone has no preference.

title: IDK
meaning: IDK stands for “I don't know.”
example: "IDK what time we're leaving yet."
context: It is one of the most common text-message abbreviations and can sound casual, uncertain or dismissive depending on tone.

title: IMHO
meaning: IMHO stands for “in my humble opinion” or sometimes “in my honest opinion.”
example: "IMHO, that restaurant is massively overrated."
context: The abbreviation is similar to IMO, with an extra hint of politeness or emphasis depending on how it is used.

title: IMO
meaning: IMO stands for “in my opinion.”
example: "IMO, the first season was much better."
context: It is a quick way to signal that a statement is a personal view rather than an objective fact.

title: Imposter syndrome
meaning: Imposter syndrome is the feeling that you are not as capable as others think and may be exposed as a fraud despite evidence that you are competent.
example: "I got the internship, but imposter syndrome keeps telling me they made a mistake."
context: It is common among students and professionals facing new challenges. The term describes a pattern of self-doubt rather than proof that someone actually lacks ability.

title: In my ___ era
meaning: “In my ___ era” means you are currently going through a particular phase, habit or identity.
example: "I'm in my staying-home-and-saving-money era."
context: The blank can be almost anything, which makes the phrase useful for captions and jokes about changing priorities.

title: Influencer
meaning: An influencer is a person with an online audience who can affect what followers watch, buy or talk about.
example: "The restaurant invited a group of local influencers to the opening."
context: Influencers can have huge or relatively small followings. The term usually implies that creating content and influencing an audience is part of their role or income.

title: Internet personality
meaning: An internet personality is someone known mainly because of their presence, content or reputation online.
example: "He started as a streamer and became a huge internet personality."
context: The term can cover creators, meme figures, streamers and people who become famous through viral moments rather than traditional media.

title: Internship
meaning: An internship is a temporary work experience designed to help someone learn about a profession or industry.
example: "I got a summer internship at a marketing agency."
context: Internships can be paid or unpaid depending on country and employer. Students often use them to gain practical experience and build a network.

title: IRL
meaning: IRL stands for “in real life,” meaning outside the internet or a digital environment.
example: "We've been gaming together for years but never met IRL."
context: The abbreviation is useful when distinguishing online friendships, events or identities from face-to-face life.

title: It's giving
meaning: It's giving is a phrase used to describe the vibe or impression that something creates.
example: "The empty fridge and instant noodles? It's giving broke student."
context: People often leave the sentence deliberately informal or exaggerated. The phrase is used heavily in fashion, memes and reaction content.

title: IYKYK
meaning: IYKYK stands for “if you know, you know.”
example: "That one kebab shop after 2 a.m. - IYKYK."
context: It signals an inside joke, shared experience or niche reference that only certain people are expected to understand.

title: JOMO
meaning: JOMO stands for “joy of missing out,” the pleasure of deliberately skipping plans and enjoying your own time.
example: "Everyone went clubbing, but my JOMO was strong with pizza and a movie."
context: It is a playful opposite to FOMO and celebrates not feeling pressured to attend everything.

title: Junior
meaning: A junior is a student in the third year of a four-year high school or college program in the United States.
example: "She's a junior studying computer science."
context: The word also has other meanings, but in student life it normally refers to year three.

title: Kings Cup
meaning: Kings Cup is a card-based drinking game where each card rank is linked to a different rule or action.
example: "Nobody remembered the Kings Cup rules, so we made half of them up."
context: The exact rules differ between friend groups, which is almost part of the tradition. The game is also known by names such as Ring of Fire in some countries.

title: L
meaning: L stands for “loss” and is used for a failure, bad decision or embarrassing outcome.
example: "Missing the train by ten seconds was a huge L."
context: Taking an L means accepting that something went badly. Online, people also comment a simple “L” when they strongly disapprove of a take or action.

title: L take
meaning: An L take is an opinion people think is bad, wrong or embarrassing.
example: "You think weekends are overrated? That's an L take."
context: It is the negative version of W take. The phrase is often used playfully in arguments about music, sports, food and internet drama.

title: Last call
meaning: Last call is the final announcement that a bar will soon stop serving alcohol.
example: "Last call was at one, so we ordered one final round."
context: The timing depends on the venue and local licensing rules. After last call, customers usually have a short period to finish their drinks.

title: Lecture
meaning: A lecture is a class where a lecturer or professor presents information to a group of students.
example: "The nine o'clock lecture was full for the first time all semester."
context: Lectures usually involve more listening than discussion, although formats vary and may include questions, polls or short activities.

title: Left on delivered
meaning: Being left on delivered means your message has reached someone’s device but has not been opened or answered.
example: "It's been twelve hours and I'm still on delivered."
context: The phrase is common in dating and friendship conversations where response times become part of how people interpret interest.

title: Left on read
meaning: Being left on read means someone has opened your message but has not replied.
example: "She read it yesterday and I'm still left on read."
context: Because many apps show read receipts, people can see that a message was viewed. Being left on read can feel awkward, though there may be innocent reasons for the delay.

title: Let him cook
meaning: Let him cook means to give someone time and space to continue what they are doing because it might turn out well.
example: "His idea sounds insane, but let him cook."
context: The phrase is often used when someone is explaining a plan, making a joke or trying something unusual. It can be sincere or ironic, especially when everyone expects the plan to fail.

title: Level up
meaning: To level up means to improve your skills, lifestyle, appearance or situation.
example: "I want to level up my running before next season."
context: The phrase comes from video games, where characters gain levels, and is now common in self-improvement and motivational content.

title: Life hack
meaning: A life hack is a clever shortcut or simple trick intended to make an everyday task easier.
example: "Using a binder clip to organise cables is a classic life hack."
context: The internet is full of life hacks, although some are genuinely useful and others are complicated solutions to problems nobody had.

title: Lightweight
meaning: A lightweight is someone who feels the effects of alcohol after a relatively small amount.
example: "Two drinks and I'm done. I'm such a lightweight."
context: Tolerance varies with body size, drinking habits, food, medication and many other factors. The term is usually teasing rather than technical.

title: Lit
meaning: Lit means exciting, fun or full of energy, especially when describing a party or event.
example: "The house party was actually lit."
context: The word can also refer to being intoxicated, but the more common social-media use simply means something was really good or lively.

title: Living my best life
meaning: Living my best life means enjoying life confidently and doing what makes you feel happy or fulfilled.
example: "Beach, no emails and good food - I'm living my best life."
context: The phrase is common in captions and is often sincere, but it can also be used ironically when the situation is obviously not glamorous.

title: LMAO
meaning: LMAO stands for “laughing my ass off” and means something is extremely funny.
example: "The ending caught me completely off guard, lmao."
context: It is stronger and more informal than LOL and contains mild profanity.

title: LMK
meaning: LMK stands for “let me know.”
example: "LMK if you're coming tonight."
context: It is a simple way to ask someone to update you, make a decision or share information later.

title: Locked in
meaning: Locked in means being completely focused, motivated and committed to a task or goal.
example: "Finals are next week, so I'm officially locked in."
context: People use it for studying, training, gaming, work and anything else that requires full concentration. Saying you are locked in usually means distractions are temporarily off the table.

title: LOL
meaning: LOL stands for “laughing out loud.”
example: "That video was ridiculous lol."
context: It started as an internet abbreviation for laughter but is now also used to soften messages or signal a light tone even when the sender is not literally laughing.

title: Lore
meaning: Lore means the background story, history or collection of stories behind a person, group or situation.
example: "Wait, you lived in Spain for six months? I need the full lore."
context: Originally common in fantasy and gaming, the word is now used for people’s personal history, friendship drama and long-running internet jokes.

title: Love bombing
meaning: Love bombing is overwhelming someone with intense attention, affection or praise very early, sometimes as a way to gain influence or control.
example: "They had met twice and he was already sending huge gifts and talking about forever."
context: Not every enthusiastic beginning is love bombing. The term is usually used when the intensity feels manipulative, disproportionate or is followed by controlling behavior.

title: Lowkey
meaning: Lowkey means slightly, secretly or without making a big deal out of something.
example: "I lowkey want to leave this party and get fries."
context: It can describe a quiet situation, but in modern slang it is often used to soften an opinion or admit something without sounding too intense.

title: Lurking
meaning: Lurking means reading, watching or following online activity without actively posting or interacting.
example: "I've been lurking in that subreddit for months."
context: A lurker may consume a lot of content while staying almost invisible to the rest of the community.

title: Main character
meaning: Main character describes someone acting like they are the central character in a movie and everyone else is part of the background.
example: "She walked through the rain with headphones on like the main character."
context: The phrase can be positive when it means enjoying your own life confidently, or negative when someone behaves as though everything revolves around them.

title: Main character energy
meaning: Main character energy is the confident, cinematic vibe of someone treating an ordinary moment like an important scene in their own story.
example: "Coffee, sunshine and that playlist: pure main character energy."
context: It is often used for aesthetic moments, solo activities or confident behavior that feels like it belongs in a film montage.

title: Major
meaning: A major is a student’s main field of study in many college systems, especially in the United States.
example: "My major is psychology, but I take a lot of design classes too."
context: A major makes up a significant part of the courses required for a degree and is usually listed on the student’s academic record.

title: Meme
meaning: A meme is an image, video, phrase or idea that spreads online and is repeatedly copied, changed or remixed.
example: "That interview turned into a meme within hours."
context: Memes work because people recognize the shared format and adapt it to new situations. They are a major part of internet culture.

title: Micro-cheating
meaning: Micro-cheating refers to small actions that may cross relationship boundaries without fitting everyone’s definition of physical cheating.
example: "Secret flirty messages with an ex could be seen as micro-cheating."
context: There is no universal list of micro-cheating behaviors. What matters is what partners have agreed is acceptable, secretive or disrespectful.

title: Mid
meaning: Mid means average, disappointing or not as good as people claim.
example: "Everyone hyped that club for weeks, but honestly it was mid."
context: It comes from “middle” or “mid-tier.” Calling something mid is not necessarily saying it is terrible; it usually means it failed to impress.

title: Minor
meaning: A minor is a secondary field of study taken alongside a student’s major.
example: "She's a business major with a minor in Spanish."
context: A minor normally requires fewer courses than a major and lets students formally develop knowledge in another subject.

title: Mood
meaning: Mood means something perfectly represents how you feel at that moment.
example: "That photo of the dog refusing to get out of bed is a mood."
context: The word became common as an online reaction to images, quotes and situations people strongly identify with.

title: NGL
meaning: NGL stands for “not gonna lie.”
example: "NGL, that was way harder than I expected."
context: It introduces a candid opinion or admission and often makes the following statement sound casual and conversational.

title: Night out
meaning: A night out is an evening spent away from home for entertainment, often involving bars, restaurants, clubs or events.
example: "Friday is our first proper night out after exams."
context: The phrase is broad: a night out can mean dinner and drinks, a concert, clubbing or almost any social evening outside the house.

title: No cap
meaning: No cap means “no lie,” “seriously” or “I’m not exaggerating.”
example: "That might be the best pizza I've ever had, no cap."
context: It is often added to the end of a statement for emphasis. The expression became widespread through hip-hop and social media.

title: NPC
meaning: NPC stands for “non-player character” and is slang for someone who seems to behave in a repetitive, predictable or unoriginal way.
example: "He says the exact same three lines every night out. Absolute NPC behavior."
context: The term comes from video games, where NPCs are controlled by the game rather than a player. Online it can be a joke, but calling a person an NPC can also be dismissive.

title: Office hours
meaning: Office hours are scheduled times when students can meet a teacher, lecturer or professor outside class for questions and help.
example: "I went to office hours because I didn't understand the assignment."
context: They are useful for discussing course material, feedback, research ideas or academic concerns without needing a separate formal appointment.

title: OMW
meaning: OMW stands for “on my way.”
example: "OMW, be there in ten."
context: It is commonly sent when someone has left or is about to arrive, although people sometimes use it optimistically before they have actually moved.

title: One-night stand
meaning: A one-night stand is a sexual encounter that happens once without an expectation of an ongoing relationship.
example: "They met while travelling and it stayed a one-night stand."
context: The term focuses on the encounter being brief and usually non-committal, though people can of course decide to meet again afterward.

title: OOTD
meaning: OOTD stands for “Outfit Of The Day.”
example: "OOTD: thrifted jacket, white tee and old sneakers."
context: People use OOTD in captions and videos to show what they are wearing. It is common in fashion, lifestyle and everyday social content.

title: Orbiting
meaning: Orbiting means continuing to watch or interact with someone’s social media after direct communication has stopped.
example: "He ghosted me but still likes every story. He's orbiting."
context: The person stays visible around the edges of your online life without actually restarting a real conversation.

title: Out of pocket
meaning: Out of pocket means inappropriate, excessive or unexpectedly outrageous.
example: "That joke at the family dinner was completely out of pocket."
context: In modern slang, it usually means someone crossed a social line. In other contexts, “out-of-pocket” can also refer to personal expenses, so context matters.

title: Parasocial relationship
meaning: A parasocial relationship is a one-sided emotional connection in which someone feels close to a public figure, creator or fictional character they do not actually know personally.
example: "Watching her vlogs every day makes it feel like we know her, but that's a parasocial relationship."
context: Social media can make these connections feel especially personal because creators share daily life and speak directly to viewers, even though the relationship is not mutual.

title: Party animal
meaning: A party animal is someone who loves going out, partying and socialising frequently.
example: "She's quiet at work but a complete party animal on weekends."
context: The phrase usually suggests high energy and enthusiasm for nightlife rather than literally describing how much someone drinks.

title: Period
meaning: Period is used to end a statement with confidence, meaning there is nothing more to debate.
example: "You deserve better. Period."
context: Often written as “periodt” in slang, it adds emphasis and finality to an opinion.

title: Photo dump
meaning: A photo dump is a casual social-media post containing a collection of loosely connected photos, often from a trip, month or event.
example: "August photo dump: festivals, bad selfies and too much pasta."
context: The style is intentionally less polished than a carefully curated single photo and often mixes good pictures with random everyday moments.

title: Pick-me
meaning: A pick-me is someone who tries hard to gain approval or attention by presenting themselves as different or better than others.
example: "She keeps saying she's 'not like other girls.' Major pick-me energy."
context: The term is most often used critically when someone puts down their own group to seem more desirable to others.

title: Plot twist
meaning: A plot twist is an unexpected development that changes how you understand a story or situation.
example: "Plot twist: the person organising the surprise party forgot the birthday."
context: The phrase comes from storytelling but is now commonly used for surprising real-life turns, often in jokes and captions.

title: Pocketing
meaning: Pocketing means keeping a romantic partner hidden from important parts of your life, such as friends, family or social media.
example: "They've dated for six months and he still hasn't introduced her to anyone."
context: Sometimes privacy is normal, but pocketing becomes a concern when one partner repeatedly avoids acknowledging the relationship without a clear reason.

title: POV
meaning: POV stands for “point of view” and is used online to frame a video or joke from a particular perspective.
example: "POV: you said you'd only stay for one drink."
context: On TikTok, POV often introduces a scenario the viewer is meant to imagine themselves experiencing, even when the camera angle is not literally first-person.

title: Pre-drinks
meaning: Pre-drinks are drinks with friends before heading to a bar, club, party or event.
example: "Pre-drinks start at eight, then we're walking into town."
context: The term is especially common in the UK and Europe and is basically the same idea as an American pregame.

title: Pregame
meaning: A pregame is drinking or hanging out before going to the main party, bar, club or event.
example: "We're meeting at mine for a pregame before the concert."
context: The goal is usually to socialise first and sometimes save money before going out. In British English, pre-drinks is more common.

title: Pro tip
meaning: A pro tip is a useful piece of advice presented as if it comes from experience or expertise.
example: "Pro tip: download the tickets before you lose signal."
context: The phrase can be sincere or joking. People often use it for small practical lessons learned the hard way.

title: Pub
meaning: A pub is a place, especially common in the UK and Ireland, where people go for drinks, food and socialising.
example: "We'll meet at the pub after work."
context: Pub comes from “public house.” Many pubs are more relaxed than nightclubs and can function as neighbourhood meeting places.

title: Pub crawl
meaning: A pub crawl is a night out where a group visits multiple pubs one after another.
example: "The society is doing a five-stop pub crawl on Thursday."
context: It is the British and Irish-flavoured cousin of a bar crawl, though the terms often overlap.

title: Quarter-life crisis
meaning: A quarter-life crisis is a period of uncertainty about career, relationships, identity or direction that often happens in someone’s twenties or early thirties.
example: "Everyone seems to have a plan except me - hello, quarter-life crisis."
context: The phrase describes the pressure many young adults feel when education ends and choices about work, money, location and relationships suddenly feel more permanent.

title: Queue
meaning: A queue is a line of people waiting for something, such as entry to a club, food counter or ticket desk.
example: "The queue for the club went around the corner."
context: Queue is especially common in British English; American English more often says “line.”

title: Rage bait
meaning: Rage bait is content designed to make people angry so they comment, share or keep watching.
example: "No one actually believes that recipe is good - it's rage bait."
context: Because anger drives engagement, creators sometimes post obviously frustrating opinions or behavior to boost reach.

title: Ratio
meaning: A ratio is an online situation where a reply or opposing reaction gets much more engagement than the original post.
example: "He tried to defend the take and got ratioed immediately."
context: The term became associated with platforms such as X/Twitter. Being ratioed usually suggests that more people disagree with a post than support it.

title: Reaction video
meaning: A reaction video is content where someone records their response to another video, event, song or piece of news.
example: "His reaction video to the final episode got more views than the recap."
context: Reaction videos are popular because viewers get both the original context and the creator’s personality, commentary or emotion.

title: Real
meaning: Real is used as a reaction meaning “I strongly relate to this” or “that is true.”
example: "I could sleep for twelve hours." - "Real."
context: A simple “real” in comments or messages often signals agreement and shared experience rather than literally questioning whether something exists.

title: Rebound
meaning: A rebound is a new romantic relationship or hookup started soon after a breakup, often before someone has fully processed the previous relationship.
example: "He started dating again two days after the breakup, and everyone called it a rebound."
context: A rebound is not automatically doomed, but the term suggests the new connection may partly be helping someone distract themselves from an ex.

title: Receipts
meaning: Receipts are screenshots, messages or other evidence used to prove what happened in an argument or story.
example: "She brought receipts, so there was no denying the messages."
context: The slang use comes from the idea of a purchase receipt proving a transaction. Online drama often revolves around who can provide the strongest receipts.

title: Red flag
meaning: A red flag is a warning sign that a person, relationship or situation may have a serious problem.
example: "He lies about small things constantly. That's a red flag."
context: In dating, red flags can point to incompatibility, disrespect or unhealthy behavior. Online, the term is also used jokingly for harmless preferences.

title: Relationship goals
meaning: Relationship goals describes a couple or relationship dynamic that other people admire or would like to have themselves.
example: "They travel together and still make each other laugh after ten years. Relationship goals."
context: The phrase is usually positive and often appears under romantic photos, although social media only shows part of any real relationship.

title: Rent free
meaning: Living rent free means something or someone keeps occupying your thoughts even though you do not want it to.
example: "That embarrassing moment from 2019 still lives rent free in my head."
context: The phrase is commonly used for songs, jokes, exes, arguments and random memories that refuse to leave your mind.

title: RIP
meaning: RIP stands for “rest in peace,” but online it is also used jokingly when something goes wrong or is ruined.
example: "My phone fell straight into the pool. RIP."
context: The original phrase is associated with death and remembrance. Meme usage extends it to minor losses, failures and broken objects.

title: Rizz
meaning: Rizz is slang for the ability to charm or attract someone, especially in a romantic or flirty situation.
example: "He didn't even use a pickup line. The guy just has rizz."
context: Someone with rizz knows how to talk, flirt or carry themselves in a way that attracts other people. The word became especially popular through TikTok, Twitch and YouTube and can also be used as a verb, as in “rizz someone up.”

title: RN
meaning: RN stands for “right now” in texting and social media.
example: "I can't talk RN, I'm in class."
context: The meaning depends on context because RN can also stand for “registered nurse,” but casual messages usually make it obvious.

title: Roasted
meaning: Roasted means humorously insulted or mocked, usually through sharp jokes.
example: "I wore the wrong shoes once and my friends roasted me all night."
context: A roast can be friendly between friends or deliberately harsh. Context and relationship make the difference.

title: ROFL
meaning: ROFL stands for “rolling on the floor laughing.”
example: "That old photo had me ROFL."
context: It is an exaggerated way to say something is very funny. The abbreviation is older internet slang and is less dominant than LOL or LMAO today.

title: Roommate
meaning: A roommate is someone you share a room, apartment or house with.
example: "My roommate keeps stealing my oat milk."
context: In American English, roommate can mean someone who shares the same home even if each person has a separate bedroom.

title: Round
meaning: A round is a set of drinks bought for everyone in a group at roughly the same time.
example: "I'll get this round; you got the last one."
context: Buying rounds is common in pubs and bars and usually means group members take turns paying.

title: Salty
meaning: Salty means annoyed, bitter or upset, often because something did not go your way.
example: "He's still salty because he lost at beer pong."
context: It is usually used for relatively small grudges or competitive frustration rather than serious anger.

title: Savage
meaning: Savage describes something brutally bold, ruthless or impressively unapologetic.
example: "She replied with one sentence and ended the whole argument. Savage."
context: The word can praise a sharp comeback or fearless action, although it can also describe behavior that is genuinely harsh.

title: Screenshotting
meaning: Screenshotting means saving an image of what is currently displayed on a phone or computer screen.
example: "I started screenshotting the messages because I knew he'd delete them."
context: Screenshots are commonly used to save posts, messages, tickets or evidence. On some apps, the other person may be notified when certain content is screenshotted.

title: Seeing someone
meaning: Seeing someone means regularly dating or spending romantic time with a person, often before the relationship has a formal label.
example: "I'm seeing someone at the moment, but it's still early."
context: The phrase is intentionally vague and can describe anything from a few dates to a more established romantic connection.

title: Seminar
meaning: A seminar is a smaller class built around discussion, analysis and active participation.
example: "We had to discuss the article in a two-hour seminar."
context: Compared with a lecture, a seminar usually has fewer students and expects more conversation, questions and preparation.

title: Sending me
meaning: Sending me means something is making you laugh very hard or causing a strong amused reaction.
example: "The way he just walked away is sending me."
context: It usually appears as “this is sending me” or “you're sending me” and is a playful online reaction.

title: Senior
meaning: A senior is a student in the final year of a typical four-year US high school or college program.
example: "Senior year is basically deadlines, job applications and trying to enjoy the last semester."
context: A graduating student is often called a senior, although degree length and terminology vary between countries.

title: Serving
meaning: Serving means strongly presenting a certain look, mood or energy.
example: "He's serving 90s movie villain in that coat."
context: The word is often followed by the specific style or vibe someone seems to embody. It is especially common in fashion and queer-influenced internet slang.

title: Sexting
meaning: Sexting means sending sexual messages, photos or videos through a phone or online platform.
example: "They had been flirting for weeks before the conversation turned into sexting."
context: Consent and privacy are essential. Sharing someone’s intimate content without permission is a serious violation and may also be illegal.

title: Shade
meaning: Shade is a subtle insult or disrespectful comment, often delivered indirectly.
example: "That comment about her outfit was definitely shade."
context: Throwing shade usually means criticizing someone without openly starting a direct argument.

title: Shitposting
meaning: Shitposting means deliberately posting low-quality, absurd or chaotic content for humor rather than serious value.
example: "The group chat stopped being useful and became pure shitposting."
context: A shitpost can be a random meme, intentionally bad edit or nonsense comment. The point is usually the joke, not quality or accuracy.

title: Shook
meaning: Shook means shocked, surprised or emotionally affected.
example: "I did not expect that ending. I'm shook."
context: It is a casual, exaggerated way to describe surprise, especially after gossip, dramatic news or an unexpected result.

title: Shot
meaning: A shot is a small serving of liquor intended to be drunk quickly, usually in one or a few sips.
example: "Someone ordered a round of shots for the table."
context: Shot sizes differ by country and venue. Because spirits are concentrated, several shots can add up to more alcohol than people expect.

title: Shotgun a beer
meaning: To shotgun a beer means opening a hole in a can and drinking it very quickly while opening the top to let air in.
example: "They tried to shotgun a beer before the festival gates opened."
context: It is a party ritual associated with rapid drinking. Because alcohol can be consumed very quickly this way, it is easy to underestimate how much you are taking in.

title: Side quest
meaning: A side quest is a random activity that is unrelated to your main plan but becomes its own little adventure.
