example: "We went out for milk and somehow ended up at karaoke. Side quest."
context: The phrase comes from gaming. In real life, people use it for unexpected errands, detours and spontaneous experiences.

title: Simp
meaning: A simp is someone seen as giving excessive attention, effort or admiration to a person they are attracted to.
example: "He crossed the city just to bring her a coffee and they aren't even dating. Simp."
context: The term is often used jokingly, but it can also be dismissive of normal kindness or affection, so tone matters.

title: Situationship
meaning: A situationship is a romantic or sexual connection that feels like more than casual dating but has not been clearly defined as a relationship.
example: "We talk every day and spend every weekend together, but somehow we're still in a situationship."
context: Situationships often have relationship-like behavior without agreed labels, expectations or commitment, which can make them exciting or confusing depending on what both people want.

title: Slay
meaning: Slay means to do something extremely well or look especially good and confident.
example: "That outfit absolutely slays."
context: The slang use has strong roots in Black and queer culture and became mainstream through fashion, drag culture, music and social media. Today it is often used as enthusiastic praise.

title: Slide into the DMs
meaning: To slide into the DMs means to privately message someone, usually in a casual or flirty way.
example: "He liked three stories and then slid into her DMs."
context: The phrase often implies making the first move online, especially with someone you do not know very well yet.

title: Sliding into someone's DMs
meaning: Sliding into someone’s DMs means sending them a private message, usually to flirt or start a personal conversation.
example: "He replied to her story and ended up sliding into her DMs."
context: It is the more specific form of slide into the DMs, often implying a first move toward dating or flirting.

title: Slow fade
meaning: A slow fade is gradually reducing contact with someone instead of clearly ending the relationship.
example: "Replies went from every hour to once a week until the whole thing disappeared."
context: Unlike ghosting, which is sudden, the slow fade happens step by step through shorter replies, fewer plans and longer delays.

title: Snatched
meaning: Snatched means looking extremely good, polished or sharply styled.
example: "That outfit is snatched."
context: The slang use is strongly associated with drag, ballroom, beauty and fashion culture. It often refers to a very flattering appearance.

title: Sneaky link
meaning: A sneaky link is a person someone meets secretly for a casual romantic or sexual encounter.
example: "He keeps disappearing after midnight to see his sneaky link."
context: The phrase usually implies the connection is hidden from friends, partners or the public and is not presented as a formal relationship.

title: Sober
meaning: Sober means not intoxicated by alcohol or drugs.
example: "I'm staying sober tonight because I'm driving."
context: The word can describe one evening or a longer-term lifestyle. Some people use “sober” to mean complete abstinence, while others simply mean currently not under the influence.

title: Soft launch
meaning: A soft launch is a subtle reveal of something new, especially a relationship, without fully announcing it.
example: "She posted two coffees and a mystery hand. Soft launch."
context: In dating, a soft launch might show hints of a partner without showing their face or naming them. The term is also used in business for low-key product releases.

title: Sophomore
meaning: A sophomore is a student in the second year of high school or college in the United States.
example: "By sophomore year, I finally knew which classes to avoid at eight in the morning."
context: In the common US sequence, sophomore comes after freshman and before junior.

title: Sorority
meaning: A sorority is a membership-based student organisation at a US college, traditionally associated with female members.
example: "She met most of her closest friends through her sorority."
context: Like fraternities, sororities can organise social events, charity work, housing and alumni networks and are part of Greek life.

title: Spam account
meaning: A spam account is a secondary account where someone posts frequently and casually without trying to maintain a polished feed.
example: "I uploaded twenty holiday photos to my spam account."
context: The term overlaps with FinSta and alt account, though a spam account usually emphasizes high-volume, low-pressure posting.

title: Spill the tea
meaning: Spill the tea means to share gossip, secrets or the real story about something.
example: "You disappeared with him for two hours. Spill the tea."
context: The phrase is closely connected to tea, meaning gossip or inside information.

title: Stalking
meaning: Stalking, in casual online slang, can mean looking through someone’s old posts or profile very thoroughly.
example: "I accidentally liked a photo from 2021 while stalking his profile."
context: People often use the word jokingly for harmless social-media browsing, but real stalking is serious unwanted behavior and should not be confused with the joke.

title: Stan
meaning: A stan is an extremely devoted fan of a celebrity, artist, team or other public figure.
example: "I've been a Beyoncé stan for years."
context: The word comes from Eminem’s song “Stan” and is now widely used as both a noun and a verb, as in “we stan.”

title: Stitch
meaning: A Stitch is a TikTok feature that lets you use a short part of someone else’s video at the start of your own.
example: "She stitched the question and then gave her answer."
context: Unlike a Duet, the original clip does not play beside your video. It appears first, after which your own recording continues the post.

title: Storytime
meaning: Storytime is a social-media format where someone tells a personal story, usually about something funny, dramatic or unusual.
example: "Storytime: how I accidentally ended up at the wrong wedding."
context: The term is especially common on TikTok and YouTube. A good storytime usually builds suspense and keeps viewers watching for the outcome.

title: Student union
meaning: A student union is an organisation that represents students and often runs services, clubs, events or social spaces.
example: "The student union is organising the campus election."
context: The exact role differs by country and university. It can refer to the student organisation itself, a building used by students, or both.

title: Study abroad
meaning: Study abroad means completing part of your education in another country.
example: "I'm studying abroad in Barcelona next semester."
context: Programs can last a few weeks, a semester or a full academic year and may be organised through a university or external provider.

title: Study buddy
meaning: A study buddy is someone you regularly study with and help stay motivated or accountable.
example: "My study buddy texts me when I'm about to skip the library."
context: A good study buddy can make revision less lonely and help with explaining difficult material to each other.

title: Study session
meaning: A study session is a planned period of time spent studying, either alone or with other people.
example: "We're doing a study session in the library tonight."
context: It can be focused on one exam, a specific chapter or simply catching up on coursework.

title: Sus
meaning: Sus is short for “suspicious” or “suspect” and describes something that seems strange, dishonest or untrustworthy.
example: "He disappeared for an hour and came back with no explanation. That's sus."
context: The abbreviation existed before gaming, but Among Us helped make it mainstream online. It is now used casually for anything that feels questionable.

title: Talking stage
meaning: The talking stage is the early phase when two people are regularly chatting and getting to know each other before deciding whether they are actually dating.
example: "We're not together; we're still in the talking stage."
context: It often involves texting, flirting and a few dates. The boundaries can be unclear because neither person may have defined the relationship yet.

title: TBH
meaning: TBH stands for “to be honest.”
example: "TBH, I don't really feel like going out tonight."
context: It is often used before an honest admission, opinion or compliment and is common in texts and social media comments.

title: Tea
meaning: Tea means gossip, inside information or the truth about a dramatic situation.
example: "What's the tea with those two?"
context: People can “spill the tea” by sharing gossip or say “that's the tea” when stating what they believe is the truth.

title: The ick
meaning: The ick is the sudden feeling of being turned off by someone you were previously attracted to.
example: "Everything was fine until he started baby-talking to the waiter. Instant ick."
context: The feeling can be caused by something tiny and is often difficult to reverse. Online, people frequently share funny or oddly specific examples.

title: Thesis
meaning: A thesis is a substantial piece of academic research or writing completed as part of a degree.
example: "My thesis is about how people use AI in online communities."
context: The exact meaning differs between countries and degree levels. It usually involves a clear research question, evidence and a structured academic argument.

title: Thirst trap
meaning: A thirst trap is a photo or video posted partly to attract attention by looking especially attractive or sexy.
example: "That gym mirror selfie was definitely a thirst trap."
context: The term is often playful and does not automatically mean the post is explicit. The key idea is that it is likely meant to generate admiration or flirty reactions.

title: Thirsty
meaning: Thirsty means desperate for attention, validation or romantic interest.
example: "Commenting heart-eyes on every post is getting thirsty."
context: The word can describe someone openly seeking attention or showing obvious attraction. It often has a teasing or mildly critical tone.

title: Throwing shade
meaning: Throwing shade means making a subtle or indirect insult toward someone.
example: "He said 'some people actually arrive on time' while looking straight at me. He was throwing shade."
context: The phrase is often associated with clever, understated criticism rather than an obvious insult.

title: TMI
meaning: TMI stands for “too much information” and is used when someone shares more personal detail than you wanted to hear.
example: "I did not need that bathroom story. TMI."
context: It can be a light joke between friends or a signal that a conversation has become uncomfortably personal.

title: Touch grass
meaning: Touch grass means “go outside” and is usually said to someone who seems far too invested in the internet.
example: "You've written twenty comments about this argument. Please touch grass."
context: The phrase is a joking or insulting reminder to disconnect from online drama and return to real life for a while.

title: Toxic relationship
meaning: A toxic relationship is a relationship marked by repeated unhealthy patterns such as manipulation, disrespect, control or constant conflict.
example: "Every conversation turns into insults and guilt. The relationship has become toxic."
context: One bad argument does not automatically make a relationship toxic. The term usually refers to an ongoing pattern that harms one or both people.

title: Trending
meaning: Trending means currently receiving a lot of attention or rapidly becoming popular.
example: "That sound is trending on TikTok this week."
context: A topic can trend on a specific platform, within a community or more broadly across culture. Trends often move quickly and can disappear just as fast.

title: Troll
meaning: A troll is someone who posts provocative, annoying or offensive content mainly to get a reaction.
example: "Don't reply to that account. It's obviously a troll."
context: Trolling can range from harmless joking to targeted harassment. The defining feature is often the intention to provoke rather than have a genuine discussion.

title: Tutorial
meaning: A tutorial is a small-group or one-to-one teaching session focused on discussing course material or receiving guidance.
example: "I brought my essay plan to the tutorial."
context: The meaning varies by university and country, but tutorials are generally more interactive and personal than large lectures.

title: Unhinged
meaning: Unhinged means wildly chaotic, extreme or lacking normal restraint.
example: "Posting that at three in the morning was unhinged."
context: Online it is often used humorously for outrageous jokes, messages or behavior rather than as a serious description of mental health.

title: Unpopular opinion
meaning: An unpopular opinion is a view the speaker believes most other people will disagree with.
example: "Unpopular opinion: summer is the worst season."
context: The phrase is a common social-media prompt and often introduces opinions that are actually more popular than the poster claims.

title: Valid
meaning: Valid means acceptable, understandable or worthy of approval.
example: "Skipping the club because you're exhausted? Valid."
context: Online, saying “valid” is a quick way to say someone’s opinion, choice or feeling makes sense.

title: Vibe
meaning: A vibe is the feeling, mood or energy that a person, place or situation gives off.
example: "This bar has a really good vibe."
context: The word is intentionally broad. People use it for atmosphere, chemistry, style and gut feelings that are difficult to describe more precisely.

title: Vibe check
meaning: A vibe check is an informal test of whether someone or something fits the mood or feels right.
example: "He started arguing with the DJ and immediately failed the vibe check."
context: Online it is often used jokingly, but in normal conversation it can simply mean judging the atmosphere or someone’s energy.

title: Viral
meaning: Viral means spreading extremely quickly to a large audience online.
example: "Her twenty-second video went viral overnight."
context: A viral post can collect huge numbers of views, shares or comments in a short period, often far beyond the creator’s normal audience.

title: W
meaning: W stands for “win” and means something positive, successful or worth celebrating.
example: "Free pizza after the exam? Massive W."
context: People use W as a reaction to good news, smart decisions or impressive performances. The opposite is L, meaning loss.

title: W take
meaning: A W take is an opinion people think is good, sensible or correct.
example: "Saying fries are better with mayo? W take."
context: The phrase combines W, meaning win, with “take,” meaning opinion. It is especially common in comment sections and discussions.

title: Walk of shame
meaning: Walk of shame is a joking phrase for travelling home the morning after spending the night somewhere unexpectedly, often still wearing the previous night’s clothes.
example: "I saw three people doing the walk of shame on my way to brunch."
context: The phrase can be judgmental, so many people use it only jokingly about themselves or friends.

title: Wild
meaning: Wild means surprising, extreme, unbelievable or out of control.
example: "You met him yesterday and you're already going on holiday together? Wild."
context: It is a flexible reaction word that can express shock, amusement or disbelief.

title: Work-life balance
meaning: Work-life balance is the ability to manage work alongside rest, relationships, health and personal life.
example: "Remote work improved my work-life balance."
context: There is no perfect formula. Good balance usually means work does not consistently crowd out everything else that matters.

title: WTF
meaning: WTF stands for “what the fuck” and expresses shock, confusion or disbelief.
example: "WTF just happened?"
context: It is common online but vulgar, so it may not fit formal or professional contexts.

title: WTF moment
meaning: A WTF moment is a situation so strange, shocking or confusing that your first reaction is basically “what the fuck?”
example: "The lights went out and the DJ kept playing - total WTF moment."
context: The phrase is used for bizarre plot twists, unexpected real-life events and anything that briefly leaves people speechless.

title: Yap
meaning: To yap is to talk continuously or at length, often in a casual or rambling way.
example: "I could yap about that show all day."
context: The word is closely related to yapping and became especially common as self-aware internet slang for talking too much.

title: Yapping
meaning: Yapping means talking a lot, especially about something other people may not find important.
example: "We asked one question and he started yapping for twenty minutes."
context: The word can be teasing rather than insulting. People also use it about themselves when they know they are talking for a long time.

title: YOLO
meaning: YOLO stands for “you only live once” and is used to justify doing something spontaneous, bold or slightly reckless.
example: "We booked the last-minute flight. YOLO."
context: The phrase became especially popular in the early 2010s. It can encourage adventure, but it is also often used ironically for very small decisions.

title: Zombieing
meaning: Zombieing is when someone who previously ghosted you suddenly returns and starts contacting you again.
example: "Three months after disappearing, he texted 'hey stranger.' Classic zombieing."
context: Like a zombie coming back from the dead, the person reappears after the relationship or conversation seemed finished.
